interviewQuestions.question: What self-checks do you run on yourself mid-interview to catch common mistakes before the interviewer has to point them out?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I run a short mental checklist at roughly the halfway point, not continuously, since checking too often would itself eat into the time I'm trying to protect. First: can I name the one or two numbers or constraints that most shape this specific design — if not, I probably designed before I had them. Second: does every non-trivial component I've added have a one-sentence reason tied to a stated requirement, or did some sneak in as "the standard piece"?

Third, and easiest to miss in the moment: did the interviewer ask a question I acknowledged but never actually came back to? I'll explicitly scan my last few exchanges for that. If I find a gap in any of these, I say so directly — "actually, let me revisit this part, I don't think I justified it" — rather than letting it ride.

**Testing:** whether you can self-audit your own interview performance in real time instead of relying entirely on the interviewer to catch issues.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Mid-interview self-check habit

interviewQuestions.question: What's the difference between healthy scope-narrowing and the over-engineering mistake, since both involve leaving things out or adding complexity?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
Scope-narrowing removes features or edge cases explicitly and says so out loud — "I'll set aside notifications for now." Over-engineering is the opposite direction: adding architectural complexity that the stated requirements don't call for, usually silently, because it's part of a template for "how this kind of system is built at scale."

The test I use is whether I can point at a specific requirement that necessitates each piece of complexity. If a design has sharding, I should be able to say which stated number makes a single database insufficient. If I can't, that's a sign the complexity came from pattern-matching to a famous system rather than from this interview's actual constraints.

Both mistakes are really the same root issue in opposite directions: doing something the requirements didn't call for, whether that's skipping a needed piece or adding an unneeded one.

**Testing:** whether you understand that both over- and under-building stem from not tracing decisions back to requirements.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Distinguishing scoping from over-engineering

interviewQuestions.question: You notice partway through that you've been ignoring a hint the interviewer dropped a few minutes ago. What do you do?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I name it directly rather than letting it quietly pass a second time: "Actually, I want to go back to something you asked a few minutes ago about node failure — I don't think I addressed it." Calling it out myself, even late, reads much better than the interviewer having to repeat the question.

I'd then actually answer it, briefly, before returning to whatever I was doing when I noticed — not just acknowledge it a second time and continue on my original track again. If addressing it changes something already on the diagram, I'd point at the specific affected part rather than redrawing everything.

I treat this as a normal, recoverable slip, not something to apologize for at length — a short correction and moving on reads far better than dwelling on the miss.

**Testing:** whether you can course-correct on your own initiative instead of needing to be redirected twice.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Catching a missed interviewer hint
